bib.title: Search-R1: Training LLMs to Reason and Leverage Search Engines with Reinforcement Learning

question: Can an LLM learn, with outcome-only RL, to interleave reasoning with multi-turn calls to a real search engine?
hypothesis: Prompting reasoning LLMs to use search is suboptimal; RL with a simple outcome reward and retrieved-token loss masking will teach better search-and-reasoning behaviour than RAG, prompting, SFT or RL without search.
contributions: Analyses the challenges and gives perspectives on RL for reasoning with search engine results.
Proposes SEARCH-R1: RL with LLM rollouts interleaved with a search engine, retrieved token masking, multi-turn interleaved reasoning and search, and an outcome reward.
Systematic experiments on seven QA datasets, plus insights on RL method choice, base vs instruct LLMs and response length.

method.summary: The search engine is part of the RL environment. The policy writes <think>, <search> and <answer> segments, retrieved passages are inserted between <information> tags and masked out of the PPO or GRPO loss, and the reward is exact match on the final answer. Trained on merged NQ and HotpotQA with Qwen2.5 3B/7B (and 14B in the appendix), with an E5 retriever over 2018 Wikipedia.
method.task: open-domain and multi-hop question answering with a search tool

datasets.name: NQ + HotpotQA (merged training sets)
datasets.split: training sets of NQ and HotpotQA merged
datasets.source: Kwiatkowski et al. 2019; Yang et al. 2018

datasets.name: NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, Musique, Bamboogle
datasets.split: test or validation sets; NQ and HotpotQA in-domain, other five out-of-domain

training.objective: PPO (default) or GRPO with retrieved-token loss masking; reward = exact match of extracted answer to gold, no format reward, no neural reward model
training.warmup: warm-up ratio 0.285 (policy) and 0.015 (value) for PPO; 0.285 for GRPO
training.steps: 500 (checkpoint every 100 steps; last stable checkpoint used if training diverges)
training.seq_len: max sequence length 4,096 tokens; max response length 500; max retrieved content 500 tokens
training.regularisation: KL coefficient beta 0.001, clip ratio epsilon 0.2
training.hardware: single node, 8 H100 GPUs; gradient checkpointing; FSDP with CPU offloading

other.rollout: vLLM, tensor parallel size 1, GPU memory utilisation 0.6

inference.decoding: rollout sampling during training; evaluation decoding not stated
inference.max_tokens: max response length 500 tokens; max 500 tokens retrieved content
inference.retrieval: E5 over 2018 Wikipedia dump, top 3 passages (ablation top-k 1, 3, 5); max 4 actions

metrics.name: Exact Match (EM)
metrics.definition: exact string match of final answer to gold, following Yu et al. 2024

eval.protocol: single run per setting reported; no seeds, variance or significance tests stated; inference-style baselines use instruct models; rejection sampling generates five candidates per training prompt with instructed LLMs

prompts.text: Answer the given question. You must conduct reasoning inside <think> and </think> first every time you get new information. After reasoning, if you find you lack some knowledge, you can call a search engine by <search> query </search>, and it will return the top searched results between <information> and </information>. You can search as many times as you want. If you find no further external knowledge needed, you can directly provide the answer inside <answer> and </answer> without detailed illustrations. For example, <answer> xxx </answer>. Question: question.

evidence.quote: The maximum action budget B is set to 4, and we retrieve the top 3 passages by default.

results.claim: Search-R1 improves average relative performance over RAG baselines by 24% with Qwen2.5-7B and 20% with Qwen2.5-3B.
results.setup: Seven QA datasets, same retriever, training data and base LLMs, E5 over 2018 Wikipedia, top-3 passages, PPO default.
results.quote: We achieve 24% and 20% average relative improvement with Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-3B, respectively.
results.note: The contributions list says 41% and 20% average relative improvement; the abstract says 24% and 20%.

results.claim: Search-R1-base (PPO) on Qwen2.5-7B reaches 0.431 average EM versus 0.304 for RAG.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Base, PPO, trained on NQ+HotpotQA, RAG baseline uses instruct model, top-3 E5 over Wikipedia.
results.table: Table 2, row Search-R1-base (Qwen2.5-7b), column Avg. = 0.431; row RAG column Avg. = 0.304

results.claim: Rejection sampling with the same search loop reaches 0.348 average EM at 7B.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-7B, five candidates per training prompt, correct trajectories used for fine-tuning.
results.table: Table 2, row Rejection Sampling (Qwen2.5-7b), column Avg.

results.claim: Removing retrieved-token loss masking lowers average EM from 0.431 to 0.343.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Base, PPO; at 3B-Base the drop is 0.303 to 0.262.
results.table: Table 4, row SEARCH-R1 w.o. mask, column Avg.

results.claim: PPO reached 0.431 and GRPO 0.350 average EM for Qwen2.5-7B-Base; for 7B-Instruct GRPO 0.396 beat PPO 0.385.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Base, SEARCH-R1 GRPO group size 5, same data and retriever.
results.note: Mixed outcome across model variants; the text says final training rewards are comparable.

results.claim: GRPO converges faster than PPO but suffers reward collapse over extended training, while PPO stays stable.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-3B/7B, base and instruct, training reward curves.
results.quote: GRPO leads to reward collapse after training for many steps, whereas PPO remains stable.

results.claim: Top-k of 3 retrieved passages gives the best average EM (0.431) versus 0.375 for k=1 and 0.400 for k=5.
results.table: Table 7, rows topk=1, topk=3, topk=5, column Avg.

results.claim: In the GRPO group-size study, group size 1 (REINFORCE) generalises best at 0.410 average EM versus 0.350 for size 5.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Base, GRPO, 500 steps, last valid checkpoint used if collapse.

results.claim: Qwen2.5-14B Search-R1-base reaches 0.479 average EM, beating all baselines.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-14B, same setup as main results.

results.claim: Instruct models converge faster and start higher, but final training reward of base and instruct is highly similar.
results.quote: However, the final training reward of both model types remains highly similar after training.

limits: Single run per configuration; no seeds, variance or significance tests reported.
Training set size, optimizer, precision and wall-clock are not stated.
Only exact-match outcome reward; format rewards and more complex rewards left to future work.
Reward collapse with GRPO; checkpoints chosen by the training reward curve when training diverges.
Authors list extension to broader search strategies, uncertainty-based retrieval, other tools and multimodal reasoning as future work.
Maximum action budget fixed at 4 turns; Wikipedia 2018 corpus and E5 retriever only.

terms.definition: ensuring the policy gradient objective is computed only over LLM-generated tokens, excluding retrieved content from the optimization process

lineage.note: Search-R1 viewed as an extension of DeepSeek-R1 Zero with search-augmented RL training

lineage.work: NQ, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, PopQA, 2Wiki, Musique, Bamboogle

figures.caption: Demonstration of PPO and GRPO training with the search engine (SEARCH-R1). During the rollout, LLMs can conduct multi-turn interactions with the search engine.
figures.why: Shows where the search engine sits in the rollout loop for both algorithms.

figures.caption: (a) PPO vs. GRPO; (b) Base vs. Instruct; (c) Response length; (d) # Valid search.
figures.why: Training dynamics: GRPO collapse, response length decrease-increase-stabilize, valid searches rising.

problems: Introduction says 41% and 20% relative improvement; abstract and Section 4.4 say 24% and 20%.
Appendix I says the case study results are in Table 20, but the R1 vs Search-R1 case study is Table 9.
Section 4.3 says Table 2 mixes Base/Instruct; Section 3.1 text says responses sampled from the reference policy though the rollout uses the old policy.
